remaining_concerns: The set is necessarily dominated by nuclear signaling and Zaporizhzhia safety coverage because that is where the strongest 2022 Chapter 1B evidence clusters.
A few useful items are secondary corroboration or interpretive follow-up rather than primary transcripts, so they are kept as context instead of retain.
Repeated wire-family coverage of the same speeches and orders was trimmed to avoid overcounting the same underlying events.
Most retained items are institutional, legal, or investigative rather than firsthand battlefield observations.
Several civilian-harm records are broad and attribute responsibility to Russian forces rather than Putin personally.
The favorable or de-escalatory items are limited and conditional, not evidence of a durable peace settlement.
Heavy dependence on NGO, UN, and rights-monitor synthesis rather than official Russian records.
Several records are thematic or annual summaries, so the set favors representative mechanisms over full event-by-event coverage.
Chechnya and regional abuses are only partly attributable at presidential level in some sources, so those items stay less direct than the central Kremlin-linked repression evidence.
Coverage is heavily weighted toward repression, censorship, and annexation; little affirmative or counterbalancing evidence was supplied.
Several source families are represented by synthesis plus one illustrative incident only; direct contemporaneous government rebuttals are sparse.
One Memorial translation pair was treated as a duplicate, and two late retrospective/context pages were dropped as lower-value repeats.
Economic stabilization is largely crisis-driven and depends on sanctions shock management rather than clear structural improvement.
Household welfare outcomes are mixed and partly retrospective, with gains alongside inflation, recession, and labor-market distortions.
Several governance findings are assessment-based or indirect rather than clean decree-level evidence, so confidence in broad institutional quality remains limited.
Evidence is still heavily skewed toward official Russian-state and multilateral baseline/context sources, so attribution to Putin remains partly indirect.
Several strong records are outcome or system-capacity evidence rather than clean causal proof of 2022 policy impact.
World Bank, UNICEF, and Reuters families dominate the non-official evidence; the record is solid but not maximally diverse.
Much of the wealth and patronage material is inferential rather than direct proof of Putin's personal ownership or instruction.
Several war-justification items cluster around the same invasion speech and denial campaign, so the record is broad but not deeply independent on that mechanism.
A few of the strongest repression items are retrospective or advocacy-based rather than contemporaneous government records, which limits directness even when the pattern is clear.
Reuters still supplies the largest share of the retained/context set, so the 25 percent cap is only narrowly satisfied by keeping several non-wire corroborators.
The evidence is strongest on war initiation, repression, and macro stabilization; broader governing competence still relies partly on indirect or institutional sources.
